relationships.directAnswer: Higher bond yields can pressure stock valuations and borrowing costs, but stocks do not automatically fall. If yields are rising because growth and earnings are improving, that positive force can partly or fully offset the higher-rate headwind.
mechanismSteps: Safe bonds become more competitive and discount rates rise
supportingForces: Stronger growth and earnings can support stocks even with higher yields.
headwinds: Higher discount rates can reduce the present value investors place on future profits.
Higher financing costs can pressure households and companies.
relationships.chainBreaker: Stocks can still rise when stronger economic growth and earnings are the main reason yields are rising.
differentReactions: Profitable, cash-generative companies may be less rate-sensitive than highly valued long-duration growth companies.
relationships.historicalExample: The same rise in yields can produce different equity outcomes when it reflects growth optimism rather than an inflation or fiscal-risk shock.

growth.directAnswer: Yields rising because growth is stronger can coexist with rising stocks. Better earnings and demand can offset some valuation pressure from higher yields.
mechanismSteps: Higher discount rates push the other way
growth.chainBreaker: If inflation or policy tightening becomes the dominant story, the same yield increase can become more negative for equities.

inflation.directAnswer: When yields rise mainly because inflation concerns are increasing, stocks face a clearer headwind: discount rates and financing costs can rise while inflation may squeeze margins.
mechanismSteps: Discount rates and financing costs rise
Equity valuations and margins can come under pressure
inflation.chainBreaker: Companies with strong pricing power or unexpectedly strong earnings can still outperform.

fiscal-term-premium.directAnswer: A yield rise driven by heavier government borrowing or a higher term premium is usually a valuation and financing headwind for stocks, although the size of the effect varies by sector and balance-sheet strength.
fiscal-term-premium.chainBreaker: Very strong earnings growth or a rapid easing in fiscal-risk concerns can offset part of the pressure.

relationships.directAnswer: Growth and technology stocks are often more sensitive to higher yields because more of their valuation depends on profits expected far in the future. Higher yields increase the rate used to value those future cash flows.
mechanismSteps: Far-future profits are worth less in present-value terms
High-multiple growth valuations may face pressure
supportingForces: Strong earnings surprises can dominate the rate effect.
headwinds: Long-duration valuations are more sensitive to discount rates.
Financing costs can rise for expansion-heavy businesses.
relationships.chainBreaker: Growth stocks can still rise if earnings, margins or expected growth improve enough to outweigh the higher discount rate.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: For an existing fixed-rate bond, a higher market yield generally means a lower market price, all else equal. The old coupon has to compete with newly issued bonds offering higher yields.
mechanismSteps: New bonds offer more competitive income
Existing lower-coupon bonds become less attractive at the old price
Existing fixed-rate bond prices adjust lower
headwinds: Longer-duration fixed-rate bonds usually move more for the same yield change.
relationships.chainBreaker: Credit quality, maturity, call features and changing cash-flow expectations can affect the size of the move, but they do not remove the basic fixed-rate price/yield relationship.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Higher government bond yields often feed into borrowing benchmarks, so new mortgages, corporate bonds and other longer-term loans can become more expensive. The pass-through is not one-for-one.
mechanismSteps: Lenders / bond investors demand higher returns
headwinds: Higher debt-service costs can reduce cash available for spending or investment.
relationships.chainBreaker: Borrowing costs can stay relatively stable if credit spreads narrow, lenders compete aggressively, or central-bank policy affects shorter-term rates differently.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Higher real yields are usually a headwind for gold because interest-bearing assets become more attractive. But if yields are rising because inflation, fiscal stress or geopolitical risk is also increasing, safe-haven or inflation-related demand can push the other way.
mechanismSteps: If real yields rise, the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding gold increases
Safe-haven or inflation demand may offset that pressure
supportingForces: Inflation fear, fiscal stress or geopolitical uncertainty can support defensive demand.
headwinds: Higher real yields and a stronger U.S. dollar can weigh on gold.
relationships.chainBreaker: Gold can rise alongside yields when fiscal, inflation or geopolitical concerns create enough defensive demand, or when nominal yields rise but real yields do not.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Higher U.S. yields can support the U.S. dollar when they make dollar assets relatively more attractive. But the dollar also depends on why yields rose, what other central banks are doing and whether global risk appetite is changing.
mechanismSteps: Relative return on dollar assets may improve
Capital demand for dollar assets may increase
supportingForces: Higher relative U.S. yields can support the dollar.
headwinds: Fiscal-risk concerns or stronger policy elsewhere can offset the rate advantage.
relationships.chainBreaker: If yields rise because investors are demanding a larger fiscal-risk premium, confidence effects can complicate or even reverse the usual rate-differential story.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Lower yields can support stock valuations by reducing discount rates and borrowing costs. But if yields are falling because recession fear is rising, weaker earnings can outweigh that benefit.
mechanismSteps: Discount rates and borrowing benchmarks may fall
Economic weakness may push earnings the other way
supportingForces: Lower discount rates can support valuations.
headwinds: Recession-driven yield declines can arrive with falling earnings expectations.
relationships.chainBreaker: Stocks can fall alongside yields when investors are buying government bonds for safety because the growth outlook is deteriorating.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

recession.directAnswer: Falling yields during recession fear are not automatically good for stocks. Lower rates help valuations, but weaker demand and earnings can dominate.
mechanismSteps: Earnings expectations may fall as well
recession.chainBreaker: If policy easing stabilizes growth quickly, lower yields can become more supportive for equities.

lower-inflation.directAnswer: If yields fall because inflation is cooling without a major growth shock, lower discount rates and financing costs can be more supportive for stocks.
lower-inflation.chainBreaker: A sudden deterioration in earnings or credit conditions can still pull stocks lower.

relationships.directAnswer: For an existing fixed-rate bond, lower market yields generally mean a higher market price, all else equal.
mechanismSteps: Existing higher-coupon bonds become more attractive
Existing fixed-rate bond prices adjust higher
relationships.chainBreaker: Credit deterioration or default risk can still push a specific bond price down even while risk-free yields fall.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Lower government yields can reduce important borrowing benchmarks and make new longer-term financing cheaper, although lenders may not pass the full decline through.
mechanismSteps: New loan / bond pricing can ease
relationships.chainBreaker: Credit spreads can widen during stress, leaving corporate or household borrowing costs high even while government yields fall.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Falling real yields are generally supportive for gold because the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset declines. A weaker dollar can add support.
mechanismSteps: If real yields also fall, the return advantage of safe interest-bearing assets narrows
Gold becomes relatively less costly to hold
relationships.chainBreaker: Gold can still weaken if the U.S. dollar strengthens sharply, risk appetite improves, or the yield decline mainly reflects falling inflation rather than lower real yields.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Lower U.S. yields can reduce the relative return advantage of dollar assets and weigh on the dollar, but recession fear can create safe-haven dollar demand at the same time.
mechanismSteps: Safe-haven demand can offset the move
relationships.chainBreaker: A global risk-off episode can strengthen the dollar even while U.S. yields fall.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Higher policy rates tighten financial conditions. They can raise borrowing costs and discount rates, which is usually a headwind for stocks, although strong growth can soften the impact.
mechanismSteps: Equity valuations and demand can face pressure
relationships.chainBreaker: Stocks can still rise if the rate increase is well anticipated and earnings remain stronger than expected.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Growth and technology stocks are often especially sensitive to higher policy rates because higher discount rates reduce the present value of distant expected profits.
mechanismSteps: Future profits are discounted more heavily
relationships.chainBreaker: Exceptional earnings growth or falling long-term yields can offset part of the policy-rate headwind.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: A policy-rate increase can push shorter-term yields higher and influence longer-term yields, but long yields also reflect future inflation, growth and term-premium expectations.
mechanismSteps: Markets reassess future rates and inflation
relationships.chainBreaker: Long-term yields can fall if the rate increase convinces investors that inflation will fall or if growth expectations weaken sharply.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: When rate increases push market yields higher, existing fixed-rate bond prices generally fall. The size depends heavily on maturity and duration.
mechanismSteps: Existing fixed coupons become less competitive
relationships.chainBreaker: Long-duration bond prices can rise if investors expect the tighter policy to cause recession and much lower future rates.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Higher policy rates usually make floating-rate and newly priced borrowing more expensive, with the timing depending on the loan structure and market.
mechanismSteps: Household and business interest expense may increase
relationships.chainBreaker: Fixed-rate borrowers may be insulated until they refinance, and strong competition can reduce pass-through.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Higher relative U.S. policy rates can support the U.S. dollar by making dollar assets more attractive, but relative policy and risk conditions matter.
mechanismSteps: Demand for dollar assets may increase
relationships.chainBreaker: If markets believe the rate increase will trigger a sharp slowdown, or other central banks tighten more, the dollar response can differ.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Higher real rates are usually a headwind for gold because safe interest-bearing assets offer more return. The dollar can also strengthen, adding pressure.
mechanismSteps: Opportunity cost of non-yielding gold rises
relationships.chainBreaker: Gold can still rise if inflation, geopolitical risk or financial stress increases faster than real yields.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Rate cuts can support stocks by lowering discount rates and financing costs. But the reason for the cut matters: an emergency or recession-driven cut can arrive with rapidly weakening earnings.
mechanismSteps: Financing and discount rates may fall
Growth / earnings conditions determine whether that support dominates
relationships.chainBreaker: Stocks can fall after a rate cut if the cut is a response to a recession, financial accident or sharp deterioration in profits.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

normalizing.directAnswer: A rate cut made because inflation is cooling while growth remains reasonably stable is usually more supportive for stocks than an emergency cut. Lower discount rates help without the same recession warning.
normalizing.chainBreaker: A new inflation shock or sudden earnings deterioration can still overwhelm the benefit.

recession.directAnswer: A recession-driven rate cut is not automatically bullish for stocks. Cheaper money helps, but collapsing demand and earnings can matter more.
mechanismSteps: Earnings expectations may also fall sharply
recession.chainBreaker: If policy support stabilizes growth faster than feared, equities can recover even while the economy is still weak.

financial-stress.directAnswer: An emergency cut can calm funding markets, but it can also signal that financial stress is serious. The market response depends on whether the policy action restores confidence.
mechanismSteps: Risk assets respond to whether stress is contained
financial-stress.chainBreaker: If the underlying credit problem continues to worsen, stocks can fall despite easier policy.

relationships.directAnswer: If a policy-rate cut pulls market yields lower, existing fixed-rate bond prices generally receive support.
relationships.chainBreaker: If inflation expectations or fiscal term premium rise at the same time, long-term bond yields can stay high or rise despite the policy cut.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Policy-rate cuts usually reduce short-term funding costs and can lower new borrowing rates, although mortgages and long-term loans also depend on longer-term yields and credit spreads.
relationships.chainBreaker: Long-term borrowing can remain expensive if bond yields or credit spreads stay high.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Rate cuts can reduce the dollar's relative yield advantage and weigh on it, but a recession or financial shock can simultaneously create safe-haven dollar demand.
mechanismSteps: Relative yield support for the dollar may weaken
Safe-haven demand can push the other way
relationships.chainBreaker: The dollar can strengthen during aggressive cuts if global investors are seeking liquidity and safety.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Lower real rates are generally supportive for gold because the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset falls. A weaker dollar can add support.
relationships.chainBreaker: Gold can still weaken if inflation falls faster than nominal rates, the dollar strengthens, or financial stress fades sharply.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Lower policy rates can support demand by reducing financing costs and easing financial conditions, but monetary policy works with lags and cannot instantly repair weak productivity, supply problems or impaired credit channels.
mechanismSteps: Spending and investment may receive support
Growth can improve with a lag
relationships.chainBreaker: If households and businesses are repairing balance sheets or banks are unwilling to lend, lower rates may have a weaker effect.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: A sharp oil-price increase usually pushes headline inflation higher through fuel, transport, production and freight costs. The persistence depends on wages, expectations and how much businesses pass through.
mechanismSteps: Some costs pass into consumer prices
relationships.chainBreaker: If the oil move is brief, demand is weak or firms absorb part of the cost, the effect on underlying inflation can be smaller and shorter-lived.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Higher oil is not automatically bad for stocks. A supply shock can hurt margins and consumers, while oil rising because global demand is strong can occur alongside healthy earnings and rising equities.
mechanismSteps: Business and household energy costs change
Stocks react to the cause and sector exposure
relationships.chainBreaker: Oil and stocks can rise together when stronger economic demand is the main reason oil prices are increasing.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

demand.directAnswer: Oil rising because global demand is strong can coexist with rising stocks. The higher oil price is partly a symptom of stronger activity rather than only a cost shock.
mechanismSteps: Stocks can rise even as energy costs increase
demand.chainBreaker: If the oil rise becomes large enough to reignite inflation and squeeze consumers, the relationship can turn negative.

supply.directAnswer: A supply-driven oil spike is usually a clearer headwind for broad stocks because it raises costs and inflation without the same boost from stronger demand.
mechanismSteps: Margins, consumers and valuations can come under pressure
supply.chainBreaker: Energy producers can benefit, and broad markets can recover if the disruption proves short-lived.

relationships.directAnswer: Higher oil prices can increase revenue and cash flow for some oil producers, although costs, hedges, taxes and production volumes still matter.
relationships.chainBreaker: Energy shares can still fall if production is disrupted, costs surge, taxes change, or the oil rise is expected to be temporary.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Fuel is a major cost for airlines and many transport businesses, so a sharp oil rise can squeeze margins unless costs are hedged or passed to customers.
mechanismSteps: Margins or ticket / freight prices face pressure
relationships.chainBreaker: Hedging, fuel surcharges, stronger demand or greater pricing power can reduce the hit.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Higher fuel and energy bills can leave households with less money for other spending, especially where incomes do not rise at the same pace.
relationships.chainBreaker: Energy exporters or households with energy-linked income can experience a different effect, and government support can cushion the shock.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Oil-driven inflation can push yields higher if investors expect tighter policy or more persistent inflation. But a severe growth shock can create safe-haven bond demand and pull yields lower.
mechanismSteps: Policy expectations may become less dovish
Bond yields can face upward pressure
relationships.chainBreaker: If the oil shock is severe enough to raise recession fear, safe-haven demand can pull government yields down instead.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Oil can support gold through inflation and geopolitical-risk channels, but the same oil shock can raise real yields or strengthen the dollar, which are potential headwinds for gold.
mechanismSteps: Defensive demand for gold may increase
Rates and the dollar can push in the opposite direction
relationships.chainBreaker: Gold can fall even during an oil shock if higher real yields and a stronger dollar dominate safe-haven demand.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Copper does not have a simple one-way relationship with oil. Strong global demand can lift both, while a supply-driven oil shock can raise costs and weaken growth expectations, which can pressure copper.
mechanismSteps: Markets identify demand-driven or supply-driven cause
Copper responds to growth, supply and inventories
relationships.chainBreaker: Copper can rise during an oil shock if its own supply is tight or infrastructure demand remains strong.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Persistent inflation often increases pressure on central banks to keep policy rates higher or raise them, especially when inflation expectations risk becoming unanchored.
mechanismSteps: Policy may stay restrictive or tighten
relationships.chainBreaker: Central banks can look through a temporary supply shock if underlying inflation is easing and growth is weak.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Higher inflation usually puts upward pressure on nominal bond yields because investors want compensation for lost purchasing power and may expect tighter policy.
mechanismSteps: Expected real return on nominal bonds is eroded
Investors demand more yield / expect tighter policy
relationships.chainBreaker: Yields can still fall if recession risk or safe-haven demand becomes dominant.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: When inflation pushes market yields higher, existing fixed-rate bond prices generally fall. Inflation also reduces the purchasing power of fixed coupon payments.
mechanismSteps: Existing fixed coupons become less attractive
relationships.chainBreaker: Inflation-linked bonds or a rapid collapse in growth expectations can behave differently.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Moderate inflation can coexist with rising stocks, especially when demand and earnings are strong. Persistent or surprise inflation can become a headwind through higher rates, costs and valuation pressure.
mechanismSteps: Stock impact depends on pricing power and growth
relationships.chainBreaker: Companies with strong pricing power and robust demand can grow profits even in an inflationary environment.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Inflation can support the case for gold as a store-of-value asset, but gold does not track inflation mechanically. Real yields and the U.S. dollar can offset or dominate the inflation effect.
mechanismSteps: Demand for inflation protection may increase
Real yields / dollar can push the other way
relationships.chainBreaker: Gold can fall during high inflation if real yields rise sharply or the U.S. dollar strengthens enough.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: If the return on cash does not keep pace with inflation, each unit of money buys less over time.
mechanismSteps: Cash balance stays nominally the same
The same money buys fewer goods and services
relationships.chainBreaker: Cash can preserve purchasing power better when deposit yields rise enough to offset inflation after tax and fees.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Higher U.S. inflation can support the dollar if it causes U.S. rates to rise relative to other countries, but it can weaken the dollar if markets see inflation as eroding purchasing power or policy credibility.
mechanismSteps: Dollar response depends on which channel dominates
relationships.chainBreaker: If inflation is global and other central banks tighten more aggressively, the dollar can weaken even with high U.S. inflation.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: A stronger U.S. dollar is usually a headwind for dollar-priced gold because it raises the local-currency cost for many non-U.S. buyers and often accompanies tighter financial conditions.
mechanismSteps: Dollar-priced gold becomes more expensive in other currencies
relationships.chainBreaker: Gold and the dollar can rise together during severe geopolitical or financial stress when both are being sought defensively.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: A stronger dollar is often a headwind for silver through the precious-metal channel, while its industrial demand adds a separate growth-sensitive force.
mechanismSteps: Dollar-priced metal becomes costlier for non-dollar buyers
Industrial conditions determine the second part of silver's response
relationships.chainBreaker: Tight physical supply or strong industrial demand can support silver even during dollar strength.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: A stronger dollar can weigh on copper and other dollar-priced commodities, while the same dollar move can also tighten global financial conditions. Copper still depends heavily on industrial demand and physical supply.
mechanismSteps: Dollar-priced copper becomes more expensive in other currencies
Copper demand / price can face pressure
relationships.chainBreaker: A strong physical shortage or powerful grid and infrastructure demand can outweigh the currency headwind.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Broad dollar strength can tighten financial conditions in emerging markets, especially where borrowers or investors carry dollar-linked balance-sheet exposure.
mechanismSteps: Dollar liabilities / investor currency risk become harder to absorb
Capital and credit conditions can tighten
Investment and growth can face pressure
relationships.chainBreaker: Countries with strong external balances, deep local markets and limited dollar debt can be more resilient.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: For a U.S. company earning revenue abroad, a stronger dollar can translate the same foreign-currency sales into fewer dollars when results are reported.
mechanismSteps: Foreign-currency revenue converts into fewer U.S. dollars
Reported revenue / earnings translation can weaken
Multinational results may face a headwind
relationships.chainBreaker: Natural hedges, local costs, financial hedging and stronger overseas sales volumes can offset the translation effect.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: A stronger dollar can reduce the U.S.-dollar cost of some imported goods and inputs, creating downward pressure on import-price inflation.
mechanismSteps: Foreign goods become cheaper in dollar terms, all else equal
relationships.chainBreaker: Tariffs, supply shortages or foreign producers raising prices can offset the currency benefit.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Geopolitical conflict can push oil higher when it threatens production, pipelines or major shipping routes. A conflict with little connection to energy supply may have a much smaller oil effect.
mechanismSteps: Energy supply / shipping risk is assessed
Oil prices can face upward pressure
relationships.chainBreaker: Oil can stay flat or fall if spare supply is ample, demand is weak, or the conflict does not threaten energy flows.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

oil-region.directAnswer: Conflict in a major oil-producing region is usually more supportive for oil prices because traders may price a higher risk of lost production or exports.
oil-region.chainBreaker: Spare capacity, alternative supply or a short-lived disruption can contain the price response.

shipping.directAnswer: Conflict around a major energy shipping route can raise oil prices by threatening transport even if production itself is unchanged.
mechanismSteps: Delivered energy supply becomes less certain
shipping.chainBreaker: Successful rerouting or rapid reopening can reverse the risk premium.

relationships.directAnswer: Geopolitical conflict raises inflation mainly when it disrupts energy, food, shipping or manufacturing supply. The location and transmission channel matter more than the word “war” itself.
mechanismSteps: Supply / shipping / commodity costs are disrupted
relationships.chainBreaker: If the conflict does not materially affect traded supply or demand, inflation can remain little changed.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Geopolitical stress can increase defensive demand for gold, but that does not guarantee a higher gold price. Real yields and the U.S. dollar can push in the opposite direction.
mechanismSteps: Demand for defensive assets may increase
Rates and the dollar can offset that support
relationships.chainBreaker: Gold can struggle during a conflict if real yields and the U.S. dollar rise sharply enough.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: A major geopolitical shock can hurt risk appetite and raise uncertainty, but the economic effect depends heavily on location, duration and whether energy or supply chains are disrupted.
mechanismSteps: Supply or demand may be disrupted
relationships.chainBreaker: Stocks can recover quickly if the conflict remains contained and earnings / supply chains are not materially affected.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: The U.S. dollar can benefit from global demand for liquidity and safe assets during a shock, but its response can vary because the conflict may directly affect the United States or change relative policy expectations.
relationships.chainBreaker: If the shock undermines confidence in U.S. assets or pushes other currencies into a stronger policy response, the dollar can behave differently.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Conflict near a major shipping or manufacturing route can raise freight, insurance and delay costs and can interrupt access to components or commodities.
mechanismSteps: Input availability falls or costs rise
relationships.chainBreaker: Alternative routes, inventories and diversified suppliers can reduce the impact.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Heavier borrowing or a higher fiscal term premium can put upward pressure on Treasury yields because more securities must be absorbed and investors may demand more compensation for long-term risk. The effect is not mechanical.
mechanismSteps: Treasury supply / perceived long-term risk increases
Long-term yields can face upward pressure
relationships.chainBreaker: Strong safe-haven demand, lower inflation or weaker growth can still pull Treasury yields down.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: If fiscal stress pushes Treasury yields or risk premia higher, borrowing benchmarks across the economy can also rise.
mechanismSteps: Household and corporate borrowing may become more expensive
relationships.chainBreaker: Borrowing costs can ease if monetary policy or recession forces push overall yields lower.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Fiscal stress can pressure stocks through higher yields, financing costs and uncertainty, but deficits can also support near-term demand. The balance depends on inflation, growth and how markets view debt sustainability.
mechanismSteps: Stocks react to growth support versus long-run risk
relationships.chainBreaker: If fiscal spending strongly supports growth without raising long-term yields much, stocks can still perform well.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Fiscal stress can support the dollar through higher yields or safe-haven demand, but it can also weaken confidence in U.S. assets. There is no reliable one-direction rule.
mechanismSteps: Yields, risk appetite and confidence can move in different directions
relationships.chainBreaker: The dollar can strengthen during a U.S.-centered stress episode if global investors still prefer dollar liquidity and Treasuries over alternatives.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Fiscal stress can support gold through sovereign-risk and store-of-value demand, while higher real yields or a stronger dollar can offset that support.
mechanismSteps: Real yields / dollar can push the other way
relationships.chainBreaker: Gold can fall if fiscal stress mainly lifts real yields and the dollar rather than defensive gold demand.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Rising recession risk is usually a headwind for stocks because sales, profits and credit quality may weaken.
relationships.chainBreaker: Stocks can rise before the economy improves if markets begin to expect recovery, policy support or better future earnings.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Recession fear often pulls government yields lower as investors seek safer bonds and expect policy-rate cuts.
relationships.chainBreaker: Yields can stay high if inflation or fiscal term premium remains the dominant concern.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Recession risk usually weighs on oil by reducing expected transport, industrial and consumer demand.
relationships.chainBreaker: A major supply disruption can keep oil high even while demand expectations weaken.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Copper is highly exposed to construction, manufacturing, grids and industrial activity, so recession fear can weaken demand expectations.
relationships.chainBreaker: Supply disruptions or powerful structural grid / data-centre demand can partly offset cyclical weakness.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Recession risk can support gold through falling real yields and defensive demand, but liquidity stress or a stronger dollar can create headwinds.
relationships.chainBreaker: During an acute liquidity squeeze, investors may sell gold to raise cash even while recession risk is high.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Global recession fear can support the dollar through liquidity and safe-haven demand, even if U.S. rates are expected to fall.
mechanismSteps: Demand for dollar liquidity may increase
relationships.chainBreaker: If the downturn is concentrated in the United States or policy easing is much larger than elsewhere, the dollar can weaken.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Stagflation is difficult for stocks because weak growth can hurt earnings while high inflation can keep discount rates and costs elevated.
mechanismSteps: Margins / demand weaken while rates stay restrictive
Stocks face pressure from both sides
relationships.chainBreaker: Companies with strong pricing power or direct commodity exposure can behave differently from the broad market.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Stagflation pulls bonds in opposite directions: weak growth supports lower yields, while persistent inflation argues for higher yields. Which force dominates matters.
mechanismSteps: Bond prices can move either way
relationships.chainBreaker: If inflation breaks quickly, the growth channel can dominate and bond prices can rise strongly.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Stagflation can support gold through inflation and economic stress, but high real yields or a strong dollar can still be powerful headwinds.
mechanismSteps: Demand for defensive / real assets may increase
Real yields / dollar determine whether support persists
relationships.chainBreaker: Gold can underperform if policy stays very tight and real yields rise despite weak growth.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: If stagflation begins with an energy supply shock, oil and some commodities may stay expensive even as growth weakens. Other cyclical commodities can fall with demand.
mechanismSteps: Commodity responses split between scarce inputs and demand-sensitive markets
relationships.chainBreaker: A deep recession can eventually destroy demand and pull even the initially scarce commodity lower.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: High inflation can prevent central banks and bond markets from easing much even while growth is weak, leaving borrowing costs elevated.
mechanismSteps: Weak growth makes those costs harder to absorb
relationships.chainBreaker: If inflation falls decisively, central banks and bond yields can ease even before growth fully recovers.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: Stagflation can be especially painful for cash purchasing power because prices rise while income and growth are weak.
mechanismSteps: Income growth may not keep pace
relationships.chainBreaker: High deposit rates can cushion the loss, especially if inflation begins to fall.
relationships.historicalExample: Historical episodes differ because the cause, starting valuation, policy response and wider financial conditions are not the same.

relationships.directAnswer: A missed or delayed Treasury payment could disrupt the market that normally serves as a global benchmark and source of collateral. The exact form and duration of disruption would depend on which payments were affected and how authorities responded.
mechanismSteps: Specific Treasury securities may face unusual pricing / liquidity
Collateral and benchmark functions can be disrupted
headwinds: Liquidity, collateral and benchmark pricing can be disrupted.
relationships.chainBreaker: Some Treasury securities could still be sought for liquidity or because investors distinguish affected maturities from the rest of the market.
relationships.historicalExample: The United States has not experienced a modern broad Treasury default that provides a clean template for all asset reactions. Debt-limit episodes show that even payment-risk concerns can distort yields and market functioning.

relationships.directAnswer: A U.S. payment default creates opposing forces for the dollar: loss of confidence in U.S. credit can weigh on it, while global demand for dollar liquidity can push the other way. There is no reliable one-direction rule.
mechanismSteps: Dollar safe-haven role and U.S.-credit confidence conflict
relationships.chainBreaker: The dollar can strengthen during stress if liquidity demand dominates, even when the shock originates in the United States.

mechanismSteps: Liquidity, real yields and dollar moves can offset it
relationships.chainBreaker: Gold can fall temporarily if investors sell liquid assets to raise cash or if real yields / the dollar rise sharply.

Lenders and investors become more cautious
relationships.chainBreaker: Strong official liquidity support and rapid resolution could limit spillovers.
